sections.heading: Coming to the God whose name is love
sections.text:
Gracious Lord, you are love, so please receive this prayer in love.

My sins feel too many to count—more than the sand along the sea. But your grace is greater than my sin. Where I have multiplied guilt, you have poured out mercy beyond measure. Please do not deal with me according to what I deserve. Receive me because of who you are, and because your mercy does not run dry.
theological_themes: God is love; human sin is real and abundant; grace is more abundant than sin; the sinner approaches God only by mercy.

scripture_references.connection: John grounds God's love not in human worthiness but in God's sending of his Son as the atoning sacrifice. That directly supports approaching God as love while honestly confessing sin.
Paul teaches that grace does not merely match sin but overflows beyond it through Jesus Christ. This anchors the prayer's confidence that even countless sins are not greater than God's grace.

sections.heading: Resting my forgiveness on Christ
sections.text:
Father, look on the cross of your beloved Son. See the worth of his blood given for sinners like me. Hear him as he speaks for me even now.

Let the truth of the gospel reach my own heart: my sins are forgiven in Christ. Teach me to take courage, to stop pretending I can pay my own debt, and to lie down in peace because Jesus has carried what I could never carry.
theological_themes: Forgiveness rests on Christ's atoning death and ongoing intercession; assurance and peace come from the finished work of Christ, not self-payment.

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews presents Jesus as the living priest who saves completely because he continually intercedes for those who draw near to God through him. This supports the prayer's appeal to Christ's never-failing intercession.
John holds together honest sinfulness with Christ's advocacy and atoning sacrifice. That is the foundation for asking God to speak forgiveness and peace to the conscience.

sections.heading: Learning to treasure prayer
sections.text:
Your grace pours down like a waterfall from heaven, and your mercy never gets tired of doing good.

Help me value the gift of prayer more and more. Teach me to come to you as I really am: stained by sin, needing pardon, and yet invited to speak with you.

Let prayer become part of my whole life with you—the path under my feet, the hand on the door before my lips open, the light by which I see, the sound that tunes my ears, the life inside my understanding, the strength of my choices, the fire of my love, and the sweetness of what I remember.
theological_themes: Prayer is a privilege of access to God for sinners who need pardon; communion with God should shape the whole person—speech, perception, understanding, will, affections, and memory.

scripture_references.connection: Because Jesus is the great high priest, believers may draw near to God's throne for mercy and grace. This supports the prayer's confidence that a sinful person may come honestly to God and find help.
David's prayer shows desire for God affecting the whole person—soul, body, lips, memory, and trust. It illuminates the request that prayer would shape every faculty of life.

sections.heading: Asking to pray in a way that pleases you
sections.text:
Shape the things I ask for. Keep my prayers wise, humble, surrendered, obedient to you, formed by Scripture, and made more like Jesus.

Save me from praying as if I were trying to manage you. Teach me to ask honestly, but also to trust your will more than my own.
theological_themes: Prayer should be governed by humility, obedience, Scripture, submission to God's will, and conformity to Christ rather than selfish control.

scripture_references.connection: John connects confidence in prayer with asking according to God's will. This supports the desire for prayers that are submissive and shaped by God's purposes.
Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane models honest petition joined to complete surrender to the Father's will. This grounds the request to pray in a Christ-like way.
James warns that prayer can be distorted by selfish motives. That helps explain the request for wise and humble desires in prayer.

sections.heading: Trusting that you answer better than I can ask
sections.text:
Give me steady faith that prayer is never wasted. When I do not receive what I asked for, keep me from thinking you have ignored me. Teach me to believe that your answer may be larger, richer, and wiser than what I could see at the time.

Before I ever knew to ask, you gave me your greatest gift: your Son. Since you have given me Christ, help me trust that, in him, you will give me everything I truly need.
theological_themes: God hears prayer; apparent denial may be wise providence; the gift of Christ guarantees God's fatherly provision for all that is truly needed.

scripture_references.connection: Paul praises God as able to do beyond what believers ask or imagine. This supports trusting that God's answers may exceed the form of the original request.
Paul argues from the greater gift to the lesser: the Father who did not spare his Son will graciously give what his people need. This directly grounds the prayer's closing confidence.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original's confidence that unanswered petitions receive 'larger, richer answers' could be misunderstood as a guarantee of visible improvement or prosperity. The adaptation frames this as trust in God's wiser providence, grounded in Scripture, without implying that every hardship becomes obviously better in this life.

The phrase asking God to 'look to the cross' is an anthropomorphic appeal, not a suggestion that the Father needs to be persuaded against his own will. The adaptation preserves the appeal while making clear that forgiveness rests on the Father's gift of the Son and Christ's atonement/intercession.
significant_interpretive_choices: The original's vivid list about prayer becoming the path, latch, light, music, marrow, strength, power, and sweetness was interpreted as prayerful communion with God shaping the whole person—conduct, speech, perception, understanding, will, affections, and memory.
'Sin-soiled sinner' was rendered plainly as coming to God 'stained by sin' and needing pardon, preserving the moral seriousness without using archaic devotional phrasing.

'Unsought' was interpreted to mean that God's gift of the Son came before and apart from any initiative or deserving on the believer's part, not that all people receive saving benefit apart from faith.
